title: canary-decode-error-tokenization-mismatch-notes
content:
TL;DR: During a routine canary rollout of model-retrofit-v2-int8 on 2026-03-11 we observed a spike in "decode-error" and truncated generations for the canary subset. Root cause was a tokenizer/encoding mismatch caused by an incorrect tokenizer artifact (old tokenization mapping) included in the published model bundle due to a race in the packager pipeline (config drift: the 'latest-tokenizer' pointer was not updated atomically). Immediate mitigation was a canary rollback and redeploy with a verified tokenizer bundle. This doc captures detection, triage, commands used, RCA hypothesis, and proposed runbook/CI checks to prevent recurrence.

Detection and impact:
- 2026-03-11 09:04 UTC: Canary alert fired: canary-generation-decode-errors > 5% (SLO target <0.5%). Alert tied to canary subset of 100 requests/sec.
- 09:07 UTC: Observed increased 5xx-like user-visible failures (generation truncated, repeated unknown tokens, token sequences with repeated "\"<unk>\""). Latency also increased ~35% on canary machines.
- Scope: failure limited to canary pool (10% traffic to v2-int8). No escalation to full prod because automatic gating prevented promotion; but canary error rate breached abort threshold and must be investigated.

Quick timeline (local times UTC):
- 2026-03-11 08:50: CI finished model package publish (model-retrofit-v2-int8) and pushed canary routing update.
- 2026-03-11 09:03: Canary starts receiving traffic.
- 2026-03-11 09:04: Monitoring alerts fired (decode-error-rate).
- 2026-03-11 09:10: On-call SRE team paged and joined triage channel.
- 2026-03-11 09:20: Confirmed tokenizer mismatch hypothesis after comparing model metadata vs canary artifact tokenizer.
- 2026-03-11 09:32: Rolled back canary to previous model (v2-fp16) to stop elevated error rate.
- 2026-03-11 09:45: Replaced tokenizer in artifact store and re-deployed a constrained canary with explicit artifact checksum verification.
- 2026-03-11 10:05: Canary stabilized, error-rate back <0.2%. Incident declared mitigated.

What we observed (evidence):
- Error traces from canary pods showed generation outputs containing high frequency of token ID 0 (unknown) and repeated special tokens.
- Sampled request/response pairs (stored under s3://redwood-logs/canary/2026-03-11/09xx) showed decoding failures on deterministic prompts used by smoke tests.
- Model package metadata: model_meta.json in the published artifact referenced tokenizer_hash: "a3f7b2..." but the tokenizer.json bundled with the artifact had hash "4c9d1e..." (mismatch).
- Deployment logs from packager revealed a concurrent job that promoted a previous tokenizer build to the 'latest-tokenizer' pointer around 08:48 UTC.
- No GPU memory errors or weight corruption signatures were observed. Weights checksums matched upstream storage.

Root cause hypothesis (most likely):
1) Atomicity bug in model-packager: packager uses a pointer alias (latest-tokenizer) to choose tokenizer artifact during package assembly. A concurrent tokenizer publish raced and briefly repointed the alias to an older tokenizer build. The packager picked up mismatched tokenizer at package time, producing a model bundle with weights that expect a newer token mapping but shipped with an older tokenizer.json.
2) Lack of post-package validation: the packager did not run decode smoke tests that exercise a canonical prompt set and compare expected decoded tokens to detect tokenization drift.
3) Canary gating was configured to abort promotion, but the automated checks for tokenizer consistency were absent.

Immediate remediation performed:
- Rolled back canary routing (09:32 UTC) to v2-fp16, stabilizing user traffic.
- Quarantined the faulty artifact in object storage: moved artifact to s3://redwood-artifacts/quarantine/model-retrofit-v2-int8-20260311-1432/ and marked in internal index.
- Rebuilt the model package with explicit tokenizer specified (no alias) and ran an extended smoke test (20 canonical prompts including previously failing ones).
- Redeployed a constrained canary (reduced traffic slice) with checksum verification enabled; monitored for 30 minutes before wider promotion.

Commands and checks used during triage (examples):
- Inspect artifact checksums:
  sha256sum tokenizer.json
  jq -r .tokenizer_hash model_meta.json
- Compare packed artifact contents:
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-artifacts/model-retrofit-v2-int8-20260311/model_meta.json - | jq .
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-artifacts/model-retrofit-v2-int8-20260311/tokenizer.json - | md5sum -
- Reproduce decode locally against canary endpoint:
  curl -X POST https://canary.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CANARY_KEY' -d '{"prompt":"The capital of France is"}' | jq .choices[0].text
- Move artifact to quarantine (SRE permission):
  aws s3 mv s3://redwood-artifacts/model-retrofit-v2-int8-20260311/ s3://redwood-artifacts/quarantine/model-retrofit-v2-int8-20260311-QUARANTINE/ --recursive

Why weights corruption is unlikely:
- Checksums for weight files (sharded .ckpt) matched the upstream model registry.
- No GPU OOM or CUDA errors in pod logs.
- The failure mode is decode/tokenization-specific rather than arithmetic or numerical instability (weights would cause very different failure signatures).

Follow-ups and permanent fixes (PRs / TODOs):
- Enforce tokenizer-to-weights checksum validation in packager: when creating a package, compute and record the tokenizer hash and assert that it matches the expected hash embedded in model config. (Owner: Priya N.)
- Add decode smoke tests in CI: run a small canonical prompt set through the packaged model (inside CI container with the same tokenizer) and fail the publish on any tokenization/regression deltas. (Owner: David L.)
- Remove implicit 'latest-tokenizer' alias from automatic package selection or make alias updates atomic (use transaction-like rename patterns). (Owner: Infra team)
- Add SRE alert: canary-tokenize-mismatch-rate > 0.5% triggers pager (threshold tuned by product). (Owner: SRE)
- Update rollout runbook to include a quick checksum and smoke-test step before flipping canary routing. Document exact commands and where to find canonical prompts. (Owner: Maya C.)
- Post-incident blameless review scheduled: 2026-03-16 16:00 UTC (owners above).

Runbook additions (draft text to insert into Canary Rollout Playbook):
1) Pre-promotion checklist: ensure model bundle contains tokenizer.json; compute hash; run sha256(tokenizer.json) and compare to model_meta.json.tokenizer_hash.
2) Smoke test harness: execute a 20-prompt deterministic decode that asserts token id sequences (stored in CI fixtures) — fail early if mismatch.
3) Artifact publishing rules: avoid ambiguous aliases; packager should accept explicit tokenizer artifact id. If alias used, packager must snapshot and pin the token file in the package.
4) Quick mitigation steps for oncall: how to rollback canary, how to quarantine artifact, how to rebuild package with explicit token artifact, and how to re-run smoke tests.

Metrics to add to dashboards:
- per-canary decode-error-rate (percent of responses with decode anomalies)
- tokenizer-hash-consistency (Boolean per published artifact)
- canary-smoke-test-pass-rate (CI + post-deploy check)

Open questions for follow-up discussion:
- Should we enforce signed artifacts for tokenizers and model_meta.json to prevent accidental repointing? (security implications vs. developer friction)
- How long should the packager hold an exclusive lock on 'latest-*' pointers to avoid races?
- Define SLO for canary smoke-test execution time so CI doesn't slow down delivery.

Appendix: quick remediation checklist for oncall (one-liner steps):
- Verify alert and scope.
- Check model_meta.json vs tokenizer.json hashes in artifact.
- If mismatch, rollback canary routing immediately.
- Quarantine artifact.
- Rebuild package with explicit tokenizer id; run smoke tests.
- Redeploy constrained canary and monitor.
- Schedule post-incident review and create follow-up tickets.

Notes and lessons learned: packager alias shortcuts improve developer ergonomics but increase risk of non-atomic state during concurrent publishes. Small deterministic smoke tests provide large value at low cost. The canary gating prevented a full-blown outage; however, absent CI checks allowed the mismatch to reach the canary.

Contact for this doc: Maya Chen (oncall lead for incident), eng-sre Slack #oncall-sre.
